results.result: behaviorMate is an integrated system using networked hardware and software components that communicate via JSON-formatted UDP packets on a LAN. The system includes a Java-based UI, Behavior Controller (Arduino Due with custom PCB), and Position Controller (Arduino Nano with quadrature decoder) with specific technical specifications for timing, GPIO control, and position tracking.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C75 provide comprehensive technical documentation of the system architecture. The hardware specifications, communication protocols, and software design patterns are explicitly described with sufficient detail for replication. The modular design using standard protocols (UDP, JSON) is well-justified and technically sound.

results.result: behaviorMate provides a cost-effective alternative to proprietary systems, with total costs of approximately $3700 for VR rigs and $1700 for treadmill systems, using exclusively open-source software without requiring users to write code.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 provide specific cost estimates that are reasonable given the listed components. Claims C50-C53 accurately characterize the open-source nature and compare to proprietary alternatives (C51). The cost advantage and accessibility claims are well-supported, though C51's characterization of proprietary system costs lacks specific citations.

results.result: Treadmill position tracking accuracy was validated with mean lap time error of 0.102 seconds and mean position error of 13 mm (max 23 mm) compared to computer vision ground truth. A lap-reset feature prevents drift accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 report quantitative benchmarking with appropriate methodology (C85 - OpenCV for ground truth). The errors are small relative to typical reward zone sizes and mouse dimensions. C83-C84 acknowledge limitations and provide the lap-reset solution. The validation approach is sound and results demonstrate acceptable accuracy.

results.result: VR system latency between wheel movement and screen update had a median of 0.067 seconds (max 0.087 s), which is below mouse reaction time (~0.1 s). Position tracking accuracy showed mean error of 4.1 mm compared to ground truth.
results.evaluation: Claims C24 and C26 provide quantitative benchmarking data with appropriate sample sizes (n=20 for latency). C25 cites published literature for mouse reaction times to contextualize the latency measurements. The validation demonstrates the VR system performs within biologically relevant timescales. Methodology using high-speed camera and computer vision is appropriate.

results.result: The VR system uses Unity/C# (VRMate) with distributed rendering on separate Android devices (ODROID C4) for each display, achieving scalability without compromising frame rate. The standard setup uses five monitors at 135-degree angles in an octagonal configuration, with custom shader support for removing color channels to minimize imaging artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23, C95-C104 describe the VR architecture comprehensively. The distributed rendering approach (C96, C100-C101) is technically sound for achieving scalability. Hardware specifications are detailed (C21). The shader capability (C103-C104) addresses a practical concern for fluorescence imaging. The design is well-justified and technically appropriate.

results.result: Experimental validation used six adult mice (3 male, 3 female, 8-16 weeks) with jGCaMP8m injections in dorsal CA1, following standard surgical and training protocols. Two-photon imaging was performed using an 8-kHz resonant scanner with 16× objective at 920 nm excitation, recording an average of 1533±481 neurons in VR and 1057±169 neurons in TM.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C140 provide comprehensive methodological details for the experimental validation. Sample size (n=6) is modest but reasonable for imaging studies. Sex balance (C29) is appropriate. Surgical procedures, imaging parameters, and training protocols are standard and well-described. IACUC approval is documented (C125). The methods are reproducible and follow established practices.

results.result: Calcium imaging data were processed using Suite2p for motion correction and ROI detection, with OASIS for spike inference. Binarized event trains (threshold: 4 MAD) were used for all analyses. Place cells were identified using circular shuffle statistics (99th percentile, 1000 shuffles) with spatial criteria (3-25 consecutive significant bins, 50% trial consistency).
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C157 describe standard and appropriate analysis methods for calcium imaging. Software tools (Suite2p, OASIS) are well-established and properly cited. The place cell classification criteria (C148-C151) are rigorous with appropriate statistical controls. C146 appropriately disclaims that binarized signals represent true spiking. The analysis pipeline is reproducible and follows field standards.

results.result: VR had significantly fewer CA1 neurons classified as place cells (34.9%, 3253/9195) compared to TM (44.9%, 6101/13,454; z=14.96, p=1.27e-50), but place cells tiled the entire track in both environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 report a statistically significant difference in place cell proportions with appropriate statistical test (two-sample z-test) and large sample sizes. The p-value is extremely significant. Despite the difference in proportions, both systems show complete spatial coverage (C36), which is the key functional validation. The finding is consistent with prior literature cited in C43.

results.result: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA revealed no significant effects of environment (VR vs. TM) or context (familiar vs. novel) on mean ΔF/F amplitude (environment: F(1,5)=1.94, p=0.222; context: F(1,5)=0.004, p=0.954), frequency (environment: F(1,5)=4.38, p=0.091; context: F(1,5)=0.079, p=0.790), or spatial information (environment: F(1,5)=0.74, p=0.43; context: F(1,5)=3.79, p=0.11).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C42 report appropriate statistical analyses (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) with complete reporting of F-statistics, degrees of freedom, and p-values. The lack of significant effects on these measures suggests similar calcium transient properties across conditions. However, the sample size (n=6 mice, df=5) is modest, which may limit statistical power to detect smaller effects. The results are internally consistent.

results.result: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant effects of environment on place cell sensitivity (F(1,5)=9.85, p=0.0257) and specificity (F(1,5)=53.32, p=0.0008), with TM place cells showing higher trial-by-trial in-field firing compared to VR. No significant context effects were observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 report statistically significant environment effects with appropriate tests and complete statistics. The specificity effect (p=0.0008) is highly significant despite modest sample size. C41 provides a reasonable interpretation of these findings. The results are consistent with prior literature (C43) showing reduced trial-by-trial reliability in VR while maintaining spatial information encoding.

results.result: The observed differences in VR and TM place cell properties are consistent with previous findings of reduced trial-by-trial reliability in VR, potentially due to absence of proximal visual and tactile cues during VR tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing literature (citing Ravassard et al., 2013; Aghajan et al., 2015; Dombeck et al., 2010; Aronov and Tank, 2014; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Priestley et al., 2022). The interpretation regarding cue salience (C44) is speculative but reasonable and supported by cited literature (Knierim and Rao, 2003; Renaudineau et al., 2007; Sofroniew et al., 2014).

results.result: Place cells remapped when exposed to novel contexts in both VR and TM. Bayesian decoders trained on familiar trials decoded held-out familiar trials significantly above chance (p<0.05) but performed at chance level when tested on novel trials, demonstrating context-dependent remapping in both environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 describe remapping observations with appropriate statistical validation using Bayesian decoding (C160, citing Zhang et al., 1998). The cross-validation approach (C163) is appropriate. Subsampling to match cell numbers (C164) controls for a potential confound. The chance level calculations (C161-C162) are reasonable, though the TM method (track length/4) could be better justified. The finding that decoders fail on novel contexts demonstrates genuine remapping rather than drift.

results.result: behaviorMate has been successfully used in numerous published studies for diverse experimental paradigms including head-fixed navigation with two-photon microscopy, trace fear conditioning, goal-oriented learning, context switching, optogenetic stimulation, and investigation of synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C27, C76-C77, C86-C90, C118-C121 cite extensive published literature demonstrating the system's utility across multiple experimental paradigms and laboratories. The citations span 2016-2023 and include high-impact findings (e.g., C90 - first optical induction of place fields). This provides strong validation of the system's reliability and versatility, though it represents prior work rather than new findings in this manuscript.

results.result: Head-restrained setups with treadmills and VR systems have been widely used to study navigation, with spatial representations from freely moving animals largely conserved. Place cells, grid cells, and other spatial tuning properties have been observed in both belt-based and VR systems across hippocampal subregions and entorhinal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C54-C59, C91-C94 provide appropriate background context citing relevant literature. These are well-established findings in the field and the citations are appropriate. However, these represent prior work and general knowledge rather than new contributions. The claims accurately summarize the state of the field and justify the experimental approach.

results.result: The treadmill and VR systems incorporate specific design features optimized for imaging: belt construction from fabric ribbon with physical cues, vibration-absorbing design without platform beneath the mouse, goniometers for head angle adjustment, lightweight running wheel with low rotational momentum, and light-blocking head restraining bars.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82, C105-C107, C112-C117 describe practical design features with clear functional justifications. The vibration-absorbing design (C79) and goniometer positioning (C80, C117) are well-justified for imaging applications. The lightweight wheel design (C112-C113) cites Warren et al., 2021. These are reasonable engineering solutions, though some claims (e.g., C79, C82, C113) involve functional inferences that could benefit from quantitative validation.

results.result: The VR system supports rapid visual context switches, addition of novel virtual objects, and hybrid setups combining visual displays with physical treadmills. Alternative configurations include wireless tablet-based setups (5 Fire HD 10 tablets) for space-constrained environments using static IP assignment via router configuration.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 describe system capabilities that are logical extensions of the architecture. Claims C108-C111 provide specific details for an alternative tablet-based configuration with complete hardware specifications and networking setup. The flexibility claims are reasonable given the modular design, though actual implementation of hybrid setups is not demonstrated in the validation experiments.

results.result: The behaviorMate system is an open-source, modular behavioral control platform using networked hardware and software components that communicate via UDP/JSON protocols on a LAN. The system includes a Java-based UI, Arduino-based controllers for behavior and position tracking, and VRMate software for VR display rendering using Unity. The architecture is designed to be flexible, scalable, cost-effective, and accessible without requiring users to write code.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the system's functionality and design, noting it is 'thoroughly tested,' 'well-developed,' and provides 'compelling evidence of functionality and applicability.' One reviewer highlights the 'innovative approaches' including 'decentralized, Android-based display devices' and the 'Intranet of things scheme.' The modular architecture and ease of use are praised as 'highly desirable' features.

results.result: The behaviorMate system is cost-effective, with a VR rig costing approximately $3700 and a treadmill system around $1700, significantly cheaper than proprietary commercial alternatives like National Instruments systems.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize the cost-effectiveness as a major advantage. One reviewer states 'the cost-effectiveness of the system provided' as a key strength, and another notes it creates 'an invaluable resource for neuroscience researcher looking to set up a budget-friendly VR and head-fixed imaging rig.'

results.result: Benchmark tests demonstrate high-fidelity, real-time performance: mean lap time error of 0.102 seconds, position error of 13 mm (max 23 mm) for treadmill, VR latency of 0.067 seconds (below mouse reaction time of ~0.1 s), and VR position tracking error of 4.1 mm.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the benchmarking results, stating the authors 'report benchmark tests for high-fidelity, real-time update speed between the animal's movement and the behavioral control' and provide 'compelling evidence of the functionality' of the system. The quantitative performance data is accepted without critique.

results.result: Two-photon calcium imaging in CA1 revealed place cells in both VR and treadmill environments. VR had significantly fewer place cells (34.9%) than treadmill (44.9%). Place cells tiled the entire track in both conditions. Environment significantly affected sensitivity and specificity (higher in TM), but not amplitude, frequency, or spatial information. The differences may result from absence of tactile cues in VR.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, noting the authors 'nicely demonstrate and quantify reliable hippocampal place cell coding in both setups' and that 'this place cell characterization also provides a concrete comparison between the place cell properties observed in treadmill-based navigation vs. visual VR in a single study, which itself is a valuable contribution to the field.' The statistical analyses and interpretations are accepted without challenge.

results.result: Place cells exhibited remapping when exposed to novel contexts in both VR and treadmill environments. Bayesian decoding showed significantly below-chance error for familiar contexts but chance-level error for novel contexts, demonstrating context-dependent spatial coding in both systems.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the demonstration of 'reliable hippocampal place cell coding' and do not raise concerns about the remapping analysis or decoding results. The findings are treated as supporting evidence for the system's validity.

results.result: The behaviorMate system has been successfully used in numerous published studies for diverse experimental paradigms including head-fixed navigation with 2-photon imaging, trace fear conditioning, goal-oriented learning, optogenetic stimulation, and investigation of synaptic plasticity mechanisms. The current validation used six mice (balanced for sex) with jGCaMP8m imaging in dorsal CA1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge the extensive validation, noting 'many published studies have relied on this system' and that the design 'has been validated by the myriad experimental paradigms that have been successfully implemented.' The experimental methods for the current study are accepted without critique.

results.result: The treadmill system design features a belt-based platform without support directly beneath the mouse to reduce vibrations, adjustable goniometers for head angle optimization, sliding frame for belt tension adjustment, and a lap-reset feature to prevent position tracking drift. Belts can be customized with various tactile cues.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the treadmill design as part of the overall system validation. One reviewer specifically mentions 'the computer vision-based calibration of treadmill' as an 'innovative approach.' The design features are not questioned or critiqued.

results.result: The VR system uses five monitors in an octagonal configuration (135° between displays) positioned to align with mouse visual field. Alternative tablet-based wireless configurations are available for space-constrained setups. The system supports hybrid setups combining visual and tactile cues, and custom shaders can filter specific colors to minimize imaging artifacts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the VR implementation, noting it 'relies on Unity, a common game development engine, but implements all scene generation and customizability in the authors' behaviorMate and VRMate software.' The flexibility and innovative features are praised without critique of the specific hardware configurations.

results.result: Head-restrained navigation systems address the challenge of studying neural circuits during behavior while enabling advanced imaging techniques. Spatial representations from freely moving animals (place cells, grid cells) are conserved in head-restrained VR and treadmill setups, validating these approaches for studying hippocampal and entorhinal cortex function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these background claims as established context for the work. The manuscript's citations to prior literature supporting conservation of spatial representations in head-fixed setups are not questioned, and reviewers acknowledge the system addresses an important methodological need in the field.

results.result: Detailed methods for animal preparation, 2-photon imaging, calcium signal processing (Suite2p, OASIS), place cell classification, and Bayesian decoding analysis. All experiments followed NIH guidelines with Columbia University IACUC approval. Analysis used binarized event signals with specific thresholds and spatial binning parameters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the experimental methods or analysis approaches. The documentation is implicitly accepted as adequate, with one reviewer noting 'Documentation for installing and operating behaviorMate is available via the authors' lab website and Github.' The methods are treated as standard and appropriate for the field.

results.result: Other open-source behavioral control systems exist, but behaviorMate distinguishes itself by not requiring users to write code and using compiled Arduino programs to maximize performance without interpreter overhead.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this distinction, with one noting the 'Plug & Play feature requiring no coding experience' as an advantage. The comparison to other systems is accepted as a valid positioning of the contribution.
